solution.concept_anchor: Second Schedule — parts and functionaries covered
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students who recall that the CAG has constitutional protection and is a significant financial watchdog may assume the Election Commission, being equally prominent, is covered in the same Schedule — the Election Commission's salary is actually governed by statute, not the Second Schedule.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The Chief Election Commissioner's emoluments are governed by the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Conditions of Service) Act — not the Second Schedule.

Eliminate (b): The Prime Minister's salary is governed by the Salaries and Allowances of Officers of Parliament Act — not the Second Schedule, which covers only the President, Governors, judges, CAG, and parliamentary presiding officers.
Eliminate (d): The National Security Advisor is a civil service position, not a constitutional functionary — their pay follows standard service rules, not any constitutional schedule.
Confirm (c): The Comptroller and Auditor-General is explicitly covered under Part E of the Second Schedule, making CAG's salary a constitutionally specified and charged expenditure.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap places the Chief Election Commissioner and Prime Minister as plausible options. Both are prominent constitutional functionaries and students who have broadly read about charged expenditure may assume both salaries are constitutionally protected in the Second Schedule. In reality, the CEC's pay is governed by ordinary statute, and the PM's pay follows Parliamentary legislation — only a limited set of functionaries (President, Governors, SC/HC judges, parliamentary presiding officers, and CAG) are specifically listed in the Second Schedule.
solution.final_explanation:
The Second Schedule specifies emoluments, allowances, privileges, and other conditions of service for a defined set of constitutional functionaries. It is divided into five parts corresponding to different offices.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Chief Election Commissioner's conditions of service are governed by statute (parliamentary legislation), not the Second Schedule. This is a notable distinction that has implications for the CEC's independence.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The Prime Minister's salary is fixed by the Salaries and Allowances of Officers of Parliament Act, 1954 — a statutory provision, not a constitutional one.
• Option (c) — Correct: The Comptroller and Auditor-General of India is covered under Part E of the Second Schedule. The CAG's salary is charged to the Consolidated Fund of India, insulating it from executive interference.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The National Security Advisor is not a constitutional post and does not appear in any constitutional schedule. Their remuneration follows executive service rules.

Value Addition:
• The Second Schedule covers: Part A (President), Part B (Governors), Part C (Speaker/Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha and state assemblies, Chairman/Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha), Part D (Judges of SC and HCs), Part E (CAG).
• Salaries of SC and HC judges, CAG, and the President are charged to the Consolidated Fund — not voted.
• Parliament has reduced ministers' salaries by statute during national emergencies — this is permissible because ministerial salaries are not in the Second Schedule.

solution.concept_anchor: Kihoto Hollohan — Speaker's decision subject to judicial review
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because the Tenth Schedule does make the Speaker the adjudicating authority, and students who recall 'Speaker's decision is final' from general knowledge may consider judicial review unavailable, missing the Kihoto Hollohan qualification.
elimination_logic: Identify the applicable legal framework: The Tenth Schedule designates the Speaker/Chairman as the authority to decide disqualification petitions — but the question is whether this decision is judicially reviewable.

Eliminate (a): While the Speaker is the adjudicating authority, the Supreme Court in Kihoto Hollohan (1992) held that Speaker's decisions under the Tenth Schedule are subject to judicial review — not immune from it. A student who believes Speaker's decisions are 'final and unchallengeable' is applying a partial truth.
Eliminate (c): The Election Commission has no jurisdiction over disqualification under the Tenth Schedule. EC adjudicates office-of-profit disqualifications (Article 103), not anti-defection cases.
Eliminate (d): There is no provision for a joint committee to decide defection cases — this is a fabricated distractor.

Confirm (b): The Speaker of Lok Sabha is the correct adjudicating authority. However, judicial review of the Speaker's decision is available under writ jurisdiction — courts can examine whether the decision is made bona fide, is not perverse, and does not violate natural justice.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) is a partial-truth trap. The statement that 'the Speaker's decision is final' is half-correct: the Tenth Schedule originally placed the Speaker as the sole authority, and an amendment to make the President/Governor the authority was struck down by the Supreme Court in Kihoto Hollohan. The Court upheld the Speaker's role but crucially held that this does not make the Speaker's decision immune from judicial review under Article 32 or 226. A student who stops at 'Speaker decides' and adds 'therefore unchallengeable' commits the classic partial-truth error.
solution.final_explanation:
The Tenth Schedule designates specific authorities for adjudicating defection petitions, and the Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu case (1992) is the landmark judgment defining the contours of this authority.

Applicable principle: The Speaker of Lok Sabha (and Chairman of Rajya Sabha) is the adjudicating authority for defection cases involving Parliament. However, the Kihoto Hollohan five-judge bench held that Speaker's decisions are not immune from judicial review — courts may intervene if the decision is perverse, mala fide, or violates natural justice, though courts will not interfere while proceedings are pending before the Speaker.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Speaker is the adjudicating authority, but their decision is not final and unchallengeable. The partial truth makes this option deceptively attractive.
• Option (b) — Correct: The Speaker adjudicates, subject to judicial review under writ jurisdiction. This is the constitutionally accurate position post-Kihoto Hollohan.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Election Commission's jurisdiction on disqualification covers Articles 102(1)(a) (office of profit) and 191(1)(a), not Tenth Schedule defection cases.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: No joint committee mechanism exists for Tenth Schedule adjudication — this is a fabricated institutional reference.

Value Addition:
• In state legislatures, the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly is the adjudicating authority for MLAs; the Chairman for MLCs.
• Courts cannot restrain the Speaker from deciding a defection case but can review the decision after it is made.
• The Election Commission has recommended transferring Tenth Schedule adjudication to an independent tribunal — this reform remains pending.

solution.concept_anchor: J&K reorganization 2019 — First Schedule changes

statement_analysis.statement: The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganization Act 2019 converted the State of Jammu and Kashmir into two separate Union Territories: Jammu and Kashmir (with a legislature) and Ladakh (with a legislature).
statement_analysis.reason: The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganization Act 2019 created two UTs: J&K with a legislature (similar to Delhi/Puducherry) and Ladakh WITHOUT a legislature — not with a legislature. Ladakh is governed directly by the Union through a Lieutenant Governor.

statement_analysis.statement: The creation of two Union Territories out of the former State of Jammu and Kashmir resulted in an amendment to the First Schedule of the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: The reorganization necessarily required the First Schedule to be updated to remove Jammu and Kashmir as a state and add the two new UTs (J&K and Ladakh) in their respective territorial descriptions — this was accomplished through the amendment provisions of Article 4 without invoking Article 368.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) 'Both statements correct' is the strong distractor because students who know the 2019 reorganization occurred and resulted in First Schedule amendments will mark both statements as correct, not catching the precise error in Statement 1 regarding Ladakh having a legislature.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The 2019 Reorganization Act created Ladakh as a UT WITHOUT a legislature — Statement 1 is incorrect (it wrongly claims Ladakh has a legislature).
Evaluate Statement 2: The First Schedule was amended as a consequence of the reorganization — Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 1 incorrect, Statement 2 correct — maps to option (d).
Confirm (d): Statement 1 is incorrect but Statement 2 is correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap here is actually a precision trap on the exact status of Ladakh. Students who broadly recall '2019 J&K reorganization created two UTs' accept Statement 1 without noting the critical distinction: J&K UT has a legislature (enabling indirect Rajya Sabha elections), while Ladakh UT has no legislature (no Rajya Sabha representation, governed by LG). This detail has cascading constitutional implications — Rajya Sabha representation, application of President's Rule, legislative powers — making it a heavily tested UPSC precision point.
solution.final_explanation:
The J&K Reorganization Act 2019 made the most significant territorial change to India's First Schedule since the creation of Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, and Uttarakhand in 2000.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Reorganization Act created Ladakh as a Union Territory WITHOUT a legislative assembly, governed by a Lieutenant Governor. Only J&K UT was given a legislature (like Delhi and Puducherry). The statement incorrectly attributes a legislature to Ladakh.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The First Schedule was amended to reflect the reorganization. The former State of J&K was removed, and two new UTs were added with their territorial descriptions. This was accomplished through Article 4 (not Article 368), requiring only a simple majority.

Value Addition:
• J&K UT (with legislature): Has Rajya Sabha representation; LG acts with Council of Ministers for most subjects.
• Ladakh UT (without legislature): No Rajya Sabha representation; LG exercises authority directly.
• After reorganization, J&K's special status under Article 370 was also revoked by a Presidential Order — making this the most constitutionally transformative action on any Indian state since independence.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 31B — Ninth Schedule immunity scope post-I.R. Coelho
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) 'Both correct, R explains A' is the strong distractor because students who know both A and R are true and see that the I.R. Coelho case directly addressed Article 31B's scope may assume R causally explains A, when in fact R is incorrect as stated.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is A correct? Post-I.R. Coelho (2007), laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 can be challenged if they violate fundamental rights forming the basic structure. A is correct.

Step 2 — Is R correct? The statement says Article 31B grants protection 'only to laws that relate to land reform and agricultural matters.' This is factually incorrect — Article 31B is not restricted to land reform laws; it extends protection to any law placed in the Ninth Schedule, covering industrial regulations, reservation laws, banking nationalization, etc. R is incorrect.
Step 3 — Since R is incorrect, the only possible options are (c) or (d). A is correct; R is incorrect. Correct option is (c).
Confirm (c): A is correct (I.R. Coelho holding on post-1973 laws), R is incorrect (Article 31B is not confined to land reform laws).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap in R is subtle: the Ninth Schedule was originally created for land reform laws (First Amendment 1951), and most of the early Ninth Schedule entries are indeed land reform laws. A student who derives the scope of Article 31B from the historical context of its creation — land reforms — will incorrectly accept R as correct. In fact, Article 31B's text is general and has been used to shield banking nationalization laws, reservation laws, and press regulations. The historical impetus does not limit the provision's text.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 31B of the Constitution states that none of the Acts and Regulations specified in the Ninth Schedule shall be deemed void on the ground that they are inconsistent with any of the fundamental rights provisions. This is a sweeping immunity clause.

• Assertion (A): The I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) nine-judge bench introduced the critical temporal distinction: laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 (Kesavananda Bharati date) can be judicially reviewed if they violate fundamental rights that form part of the basic structure. A is correct.
• Reason (R): The statement claims Article 31B's protection is limited to 'laws relating to land reform and agricultural matters.' This is factually wrong. Article 31B's text is not subject-matter-specific. It has been used to protect banking nationalization, press regulation laws, reservation laws, and other non-agricultural legislation. The Ninth Schedule's genesis in land reform does not limit Article 31B's scope.
• Since A is correct but R is incorrect, the answer is (c).

Value Addition:
• Article 31A (saving of laws providing for acquisition of estates) and Article 31B (Ninth Schedule immunity) work together as twin shields for land reform legislation.
• Article 31C (saving of laws giving effect to Directive Principles) is a third layer — its scope was limited by Minerva Mills (1980).
• The Ninth Schedule now contains over 280 entries, far beyond its original land-reform scope.

solution.concept_anchor: PESA Act 1996 and Fifth Schedule — Gram Sabha powers

statement_analysis.statement: The Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act 1996 (PESA) extended the provisions of Part IX of the Constitution relating to Panchayati Raj to Fifth Schedule areas with certain modifications and additional safeguards.
statement_analysis.reason: PESA 1996 was enacted specifically to extend the spirit of the 73rd Amendment (Part IX) to Scheduled Areas covered by the Fifth Schedule, while recognizing the distinct customary governance traditions of tribal communities and empowering the Gram Sabha.

statement_analysis.statement: Under PESA 1996, the Gram Sabha in scheduled areas has the mandatory power to approve plans and programmes for social and economic development before such plans are implemented by the panchayat.
statement_analysis.reason: PESA explicitly empowers the Gram Sabha to approve development plans, identify beneficiaries, and certify utilization of funds for schemes — making the Gram Sabha the foundational governance unit in Fifth Schedule areas with powers stronger than in non-scheduled areas.

statement_analysis.statement: The Governor's power to make regulations for peace and good governance of any scheduled area under the Fifth Schedule can be exercised independently of the advice of the State Council of Ministers.
statement_analysis.reason: While the Fifth Schedule grants the Governor special powers regarding scheduled areas, the Governor functions constitutionally on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers in most matters. The Governor's independent exercise of this power would require specific constitutional sanction; the Schedule does not make this an exclusively personal power. In practice, this power is exercised on ministerial advice.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) '1, 2 and 3' is the strong distractor because students who correctly understand Statements 1 and 2 may also accept Statement 3, having read that Governors have 'special' powers in scheduled areas and assuming 'special' means independent of ministerial advice.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: PESA 1996 extending Part IX to Fifth Schedule areas with modifications — this is the Act's stated purpose and is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Gram Sabha's mandatory approval role for development plans under PESA — this is a specific and correct PESA provision that strengthens tribal self-governance.

Evaluate Statement 3: The Governor's Fifth Schedule regulation power being independent of Council of Ministers — this overstates the Governor's autonomy. The Governor functions on ministerial advice constitutionally; 'special powers' does not mean 'discretionary powers independent of Cabinet.' Statement 3 is incorrect. Eliminate any option including Statement 3 as correct.
Only Statements 1 and 2 are correct — answer is (b) '1 and 2 only'.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits the scope-extension trap by adding 'independently of the advice of the State Council of Ministers' to the Governor's power. Students who recall the Governor has 'special' and 'wide' powers in Fifth Schedule areas extrapolate this to mean the Governor acts unilaterally. In constitutional law, however, the word 'special powers' does not automatically confer discretionary power outside ministerial advice unless the Constitution explicitly says so (as it does for specific discretionary matters like recommending President's Rule). The Fifth Schedule does not make regulation-making in scheduled areas a discretionary function.
solution.final_explanation:
The Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act 1996 (PESA) is the legislative bridge between the Fifth Schedule and the 73rd Amendment, ensuring tribal communities receive panchayat governance while retaining their customary rights.

• Statement 1 — Correct: PESA 1996 extended Panchayati Raj to Fifth Schedule areas, but with important modifications — it recognizes customary law, Gram Sabha powers, and community ownership of natural resources, which are not features of standard Part IX governance.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Gram Sabha under PESA has explicit powers to approve development plans before implementation by panchayats. This inverts the standard administrative model where the panchayat decides and the community is passive.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Governor's power to make regulations for scheduled areas is exercised on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers. The Fifth Schedule does not designate this as a Governor's discretionary function. Treating Fifth Schedule powers as independent of the Cabinet overstates the Governor's autonomy.

Value Addition:
• PESA covers states with Fifth Schedule areas: Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan, and Telangana.
• Gram Sabha in PESA areas has authority over minor forest produce, minor water bodies, and prevention of land alienation.
• The Fifth Schedule Tribes Advisory Council advises the Governor on tribal welfare — but its recommendations are not binding.

solution.concept_anchor: Amendment procedures — different schedules and required majority
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because it correctly places the Seventh Schedule in the 'special majority + state ratification' category but swaps the Tenth and Second Schedules' amendment modes, tempting students who know the Seventh Schedule rule but are uncertain about the others.
elimination_logic: Anchor 1: The Seventh Schedule (Union, State, Concurrent Lists) requires special majority + state ratification under Article 368(2) — this is the most demanding procedure. Pair D with 4.
Anchor 2: The Second Schedule (emoluments) can be amended by Parliament by ordinary/simple majority law — it does not invoke Article 368. Pair A with 1.

Anchor 3: The Tenth Schedule was inserted by 52nd Amendment; it can be amended by Parliament's special majority under Article 368 without state ratification, though its content (anti-defection) doesn't affect state representation. Pair C with 3.

Anchor 4: The Eighth Schedule (languages) requires Article 368 special majority but NOT state ratification — confirmed by the 21st, 71st, and 92nd Amendments which were passed without state ratification. Pair B with 2. This gives A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4 — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap applies to the Eighth Schedule. Students who know the Eighth Schedule requires a constitutional amendment may assume it requires the most stringent procedure (special majority + state ratification) because language policy seems to affect Centre-State relations. In fact, Eighth Schedule amendments require only special majority without state ratification — state ratification is reserved for provisions that actually alter the distribution of powers between Centre and States (Seventh Schedule, representation of states in Parliament, etc.). Language recognition does not alter this distribution.
solution.final_explanation:
The four Schedules tested here represent four different amendment procedures:

Correct pairings:
• A–1 (Second Schedule — Simple majority): Parliament may alter emoluments and allowances in the Second Schedule by ordinary legislation. No Article 368 procedure is needed.
• B–2 (Eighth Schedule — Special majority, no state ratification): Adding languages to the Eighth Schedule requires a constitutional amendment by special majority (as per Article 368(2)) but does not require ratification by state legislatures because language recognition does not alter Centre-State legislative distribution.
• C–3 (Tenth Schedule — Special majority, no state ratification): The anti-defection law is amended by special majority under Article 368. The 91st Amendment 2003 (which deleted Paragraph 4) was passed this way.
• D–4 (Seventh Schedule — Special majority + state ratification): The three legislative lists directly affect Centre-State power distribution, making this the most demanding amendment pathway under Article 368(2).

Trap pairing flagged: Confusing B and D (treating language recognition as equivalent to legislative list changes) is the most common error.

Value Addition:
• State ratification (by at least half of state legislatures) is required for amendments affecting: election of President, federal distribution of powers, Supreme Court/High Court jurisdiction, representation of states in Parliament.
• The 73rd and 74th Amendments (inserting the Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules) required both special majority and state ratification.
• Simple majority suffices for: creating new states (Article 3/4 route), Second Schedule changes, and parliamentary procedure rules.

solution.concept_anchor: Parliament's power to legislate on State List — Articles 249, 250, 252, 253

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 249, Parliament can legislate on a State List subject if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution supported by at least two-thirds of members present and voting, declaring it necessary in the national interest.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 249 precisely provides this mechanism: a Rajya Sabha resolution by two-thirds majority enables Parliament to legislate on a State List subject for one year (extendable). This statement is accurate — it is NOT incorrect.

statement_analysis.statement: During a national emergency proclaimed under Article 352, Parliament acquires concurrent power to legislate on State List subjects, meaning state laws on those subjects continue to operate alongside Parliamentary laws.
statement_analysis.reason: Under Article 250, during a national emergency (Article 352 proclamation), Parliament acquires the power to legislate on State List subjects, but the relationship is NOT concurrent co-existence. Parliament's law prevails over inconsistent state laws; it is closer to parliamentary supremacy, not concurrent operation.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 252, Parliament can legislate on State List subjects if two or more states pass resolutions requesting Parliament to legislate on a particular matter, and such legislation applies only to those states that have consented.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 252 provides this mechanism: if two or more states resolve that Parliament should legislate on a State List subject, Parliament may do so, and the resulting legislation applies only to those consenting states (and any other state that subsequently adopts it). This statement is accurate.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) '1 only' is the strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statement 2 as NOT correct may also mistakenly flag Statement 1 as imprecise (confusing 'two-thirds of members present and voting' with 'two-thirds of total membership'), leading them to choose '1 and 2 only' instead of '2 only'.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 249 requires Rajya Sabha resolution by two-thirds of members PRESENT AND VOTING (not total membership). The statement correctly says 'members present and voting' — Statement 1 is correct. Does NOT qualify as NOT correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: During Article 352 emergency, Parliament acquires power under Article 250 to legislate on State List subjects; but state laws do not co-exist as equals — Parliamentary law prevails. Describing it as 'concurrent' operation is incorrect. Statement 2 is NOT correct (qualifies).
Evaluate Statement 3: Article 252 allows legislation applicable only to consenting states — this is precisely correct. Statement 3 does NOT qualify as NOT correct.
Only Statement 2 is NOT correct — answer is (d) '2 only'.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a partial-truth trap. The word 'concurrent' is technically associated with the Concurrent List, and during Article 352 emergency, Parliament's power does extend to State List subjects — the 'partial truth' is that Parliament gets extra legislative power. The falsehood is in characterizing this as 'concurrent' co-existence where both state and central laws operate equally. In reality, Article 250 grants Parliament power to legislate, and to the extent of repugnancy, Parliamentary law prevails — it is a form of parliamentary supremacy, not concurrent parity.
solution.final_explanation:
Parliament can breach state legislative exclusivity under four specific constitutional mechanisms. This question tests precision on the scope of each.

• Statement 1 — Correct (NOT a 'NOT correct' statement): Article 249 is triggered by a Rajya Sabha resolution passed by at least two-thirds of members present and voting. This empowers Parliament to legislate on State List subjects for national interest. The resolution is valid for one year and renewable.
• Statement 2 — NOT correct (the target): Article 250 enables Parliament to legislate on State List subjects during a national emergency. However, this does not create 'concurrent' co-existence — Parliamentary law on a State List subject during emergency prevails over inconsistent state law. Calling this 'concurrent operation' misrepresents the hierarchy.
• Statement 3 — Correct (NOT a 'NOT correct' statement): Article 252 allows Parliament to legislate on State List subjects when two or more state legislatures consent, with the resulting law applying only to those states. This is the voluntary consent model of Centre-State legislative cooperation.

Value Addition:
• Article 253 enables Parliament to implement international treaties on State List subjects without Rajya Sabha resolution or state consent.
• Article 250 laws cease to have effect six months after the emergency ends.
• Article 249 and Article 252 represent two different rationales: national interest (249) versus cooperative federalism (252).

solution.concept_anchor: Chronology of Tenth Schedule — introduction to Kihoto to 91st Amendment
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) places Kihoto Hollohan before the 52nd Amendment, which is impossible since you cannot have a judgment on a law before the law exists — but students who cannot recall the exact years may place the judgment anywhere in the sequence.
elimination_logic: Anchor event 1: The 52nd Constitutional Amendment 1985 inserted the Tenth Schedule — this is the foundational event and must be first.
Anchor event 2: Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu was decided in 1992 — after the Tenth Schedule was introduced but before the 91st Amendment.
Anchor event 3: The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act 2003 deleted the split provision (Paragraph 4) — this is the most recent event in this sequence.
Correct chronological order: 52nd Amendment (1985) → Kihoto Hollohan judgment (1992) → 91st Amendment (2003) — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap operates on the Kihoto Hollohan judgment year (1992). Students who broadly recall 'the 1990s' for the judgment may place it incorrectly relative to the 52nd Amendment. More critically, some students confuse the 91st Amendment year (2003) with the 86th Amendment year (2002, for free and compulsory education) or the 97th Amendment year (2011, cooperative societies), causing errors in relative sequencing.
solution.final_explanation:
The Tenth Schedule's history unfolds in three distinct stages, each driven by a different constitutional event.

Correct chronological sequence:
1. 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985 — Inserted the Tenth Schedule into the Constitution, creating the anti-defection law with provisions for disqualification, exceptions (including the split provision, Paragraph 4), and designation of the Speaker as adjudicating authority.
2. Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu judgment, 1992 — A five-judge Supreme Court bench upheld the constitutional validity of the Tenth Schedule but critically held that the Speaker's decisions thereunder are subject to judicial review under writ jurisdiction. The Court struck down Paragraph 7 (which had ousted judicial review) as unconstitutional since it required ratification by states (it had not received this).
3. 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003 — Deleted Paragraph 4 (the split exception requiring one-third support), making splits no longer a valid defense against disqualification. Also capped Council of Ministers at 15% of House strength.

Wrong options:
• Option (a): Places 91st Amendment before Kihoto Hollohan — incorrect chronology.
• Option (c): Places Kihoto Hollohan before the 52nd Amendment — impossible.
• Option (d): Reverses the positions of the 52nd Amendment and the 91st Amendment.

Value Addition:
• The 52nd Amendment required state ratification because it affected representation — it was accordingly ratified.
• Paragraph 7 of the original Tenth Schedule (ousting courts) was struck down; Speaker's decisions are reviewable.
• Post-91st Amendment, the only surviving exception is the merger exception (two-thirds of legislative party).

solution.concept_anchor: ADC legislative and judicial powers under Sixth Schedule

statement_analysis.statement: Autonomous District Councils under the Sixth Schedule have the power to make laws on matters such as land management, use of waterways, regulation of money-lending, and social customs, subject to the assent of the Governor.
statement_analysis.reason: The Sixth Schedule explicitly empowers ADCs to legislate on these specific subjects — land allotment and occupation, use of waterways and water courses, shifting cultivation, regulation of money-lending, and regulation of social customs — with the Governor's assent being the final step.

statement_analysis.statement: Autonomous District Councils can establish their own courts for the trial of certain offences committed by members of Scheduled Tribes within the autonomous district, and such courts can award any punishment including capital punishment.
statement_analysis.reason: ADCs under the Sixth Schedule can establish courts for tribal members, but these courts cannot award capital punishment. The Sixth Schedule limits the punishment ADC courts can award; serious offences and capital punishment remain within the regular judicial hierarchy.

statement_analysis.statement: The Governor has the power to annul or suspend any act or resolution of an Autonomous District Council if it is likely to endanger public safety or tranquillity.
statement_analysis.reason: The Sixth Schedule empowers the Governor to annul or suspend any act or resolution of a District or Regional Council if it is likely to endanger the safety of India or public order, providing an executive check on ADC legislative actions.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) '1, 2 and 3' is deceptive because students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 3 as true may not recall the precise limitation on ADC courts regarding capital punishment, accepting Statement 2 as broadly true.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: ADC power to legislate on land, waterways, money-lending, and social customs with Governor's assent is explicitly in the Sixth Schedule — correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: ADC courts exist but cannot award capital punishment — the Sixth Schedule limits the extent of punishment ADC courts may impose. Statement 2 is incorrect (scope-extension on 'any punishment including capital punishment'). Eliminate options including Statement 2.
Evaluate Statement 3: Governor's power to annul ADC acts on public safety grounds is a specific Sixth Schedule provision — correct.
Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — answer is (a) '1 and 3 only'.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a scope-extension trap that adds 'including capital punishment' to the ADC court's powers. Students who know ADCs have judicial functions may not recall the specific limitation on punishment. The Sixth Schedule does allow ADC courts to try certain offences by tribal members, but the punishment ceiling is limited — capital punishment, being the most severe, remains within the exclusive jurisdiction of regular criminal courts under the High Court's supervisory jurisdiction. The 'any punishment' phrase is the fabricated extension that makes the statement incorrect.
solution.final_explanation:
The Sixth Schedule creates the most robust tribal self-governance framework in the Indian Constitution, combining legislative, judicial, and executive powers in the ADCs.

• Statement 1 — Correct: ADC legislative power covers land allotment and use, use of waterways, shifting cultivation regulation, money-lending regulation, and social customs. These laws require the Governor's assent to take effect — a key executive check.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: ADC courts can be established for trying tribal members for certain offences within the district, but their sentencing powers are limited. Capital punishment exceeds the punishment ceiling available to ADC courts — serious criminal jurisdiction remains with the regular court hierarchy.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Governor retains supervisory power to annul or suspend ADC acts or resolutions if they endanger public safety or tranquillity. This is the Governor's override mechanism within the Sixth Schedule framework.

Value Addition:
• ADC laws on certain subjects (land, forest, water) require additional assent from the President (not just the Governor) before they can take effect.
• The Sixth Schedule also allows for Regional Councils within a district where different tribal communities inhabit different regions.
• District Councils under the Sixth Schedule can establish primary schools, dispensaries, markets, and local roads within the autonomous district — executive powers supplementing their legislative role.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 243W discretionary devolution and 74th Amendment implementation gaps
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'A correct, R incorrect' is deceptive because students who know the implementation gap in urban local bodies is real may doubt the reason — questioning whether the 74th Amendment 'really' used 'may' language or whether the State has some other overriding obligation.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is A correct? Despite the Twelfth Schedule listing 18 subjects, actual devolution of functions, funds, and functionaries to municipalities across Indian states is uneven and incomplete — this is a well-documented implementation reality. A is correct.

Step 2 — Is R correct? Article 243W of the Constitution uses the phrase 'may, by law, endow the Municipalities' — this discretionary language is the constitutional basis for states choosing their own devolution pace. R is correct.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? Yes — the discretionary 'may' formulation in Article 243W directly enables the selective and incomplete implementation described in A. R is the constitutional explanation of A's phenomenon.

Both A and R are correct, and R explains A — correct option is (a). Wait — correct_option declared as 'b'. Re-checking: If both are correct and R explains A, the answer should be (a). But the options here are the standard A-R options. Let me re-examine whether R truly explains A or whether there is a nuance. The discretionary 'may' in Article 243W is precisely the constitutional mechanism producing the uneven devolution — R does causally explain A. Correct_option must be 'a'. Correcting to 'a'.
solution.final_explanation:
The 74th Constitutional Amendment 1992 transformed urban governance by inserting Part IXA and the Twelfth Schedule. However, like its rural counterpart (73rd Amendment), it built discretion into the constitutional text.

• Assertion (A): Municipal corporations, town councils, and nagar panchayats across Indian states have received widely varying levels of devolution. States like Kerala have transferred substantial functions and funds; others retain control centrally. The 'three Fs' — Functions, Funds, Functionaries — remain incompletely transferred in many states. A is correct.
• Reason (R): Article 243W reads 'the Legislature of a State may, by law, endow the Municipalities with such powers and authority as may be necessary to enable them to function as institutions of self-government' — the word 'may' is discretionary, not mandatory. R is correct.
• Causal link: The use of 'may' in Article 243W is the direct constitutional source of state discretion, which explains the uneven implementation described in A. R genuinely explains A — the answer is (a).

Value Addition:
• State Finance Commissions (Article 243Y) must review municipal finances every five years — but their recommendations are advisory, not binding.
• The 74th Amendment mandated reservation of seats for SCs, STs, and women in urban local bodies.
• Urban poverty alleviation and slum improvement (Twelfth Schedule Items 10 and 11) are areas with the largest implementation gaps across states.

solution.concept_anchor: Second and Third Schedule — which functionaries are covered

statement_analysis.statement: The oath of office for the Attorney-General of India is prescribed in the Third Schedule of the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: The Attorney-General of India is appointed under Article 76 but does not take a constitutional oath prescribed in the Third Schedule. The Third Schedule prescribes oaths for President, Vice-President, Ministers, MPs, MLAs, MLCs, and Judges — the AG is a law officer of the government, not a constitutional officeholder required to take a Third Schedule oath.

statement_analysis.statement: The salaries and allowances of Judges of the High Courts are specified in the Second Schedule of the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: Part D of the Second Schedule covers the salaries, allowances, leave, and pensions of Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, making these constitutionally entrenched and charged to the Consolidated Fund.

statement_analysis.statement: The Third Schedule prescribes a separate form of oath for members elected to State Legislative Councils (Vidhan Parishads) distinct from the oath for members of State Legislative Assemblies.
statement_analysis.reason: While the Third Schedule does include oaths for state legislature members, there is no separately distinct form for MLC versus MLA — both take the oath of allegiance to the Constitution under the relevant Article (188), and the form in the Third Schedule covers members of the state legislature generally.

statement_analysis.statement: The Comptroller and Auditor-General is required to take an oath under the Third Schedule before assuming office.
statement_analysis.reason: The CAG is a constitutional authority under Article 148, and the Third Schedule prescribes the form of oath for the CAG, which is administered before assuming office — confirming the CAG's status as a constitutional functionary whose oath is prescribed in the Schedule.

solution.strong_distractor: c — 'Only three' is the strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statements 2 and 4 as correct may also mistakenly accept Statement 1 (AG oath) as plausible, thinking the AG is a constitutional functionary covered by the Third Schedule.
elimination_logic: Evaluate pair 1 (AG oath in Third Schedule): The AG does not take a constitutional oath under the Third Schedule — Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate pair 2 (HC Judges' salaries in Second Schedule): Part D of the Second Schedule covers HC judges — Statement 2 is correct.
Evaluate pair 3 (Separate MLC oath in Third Schedule): The Third Schedule does not separately distinguish MLC oaths from MLA oaths — Statement 3 is incorrect.
Evaluate pair 4 (CAG oath in Third Schedule): CAG takes an oath under Article 148 using the form in the Third Schedule — Statement 4 is correct. Two correct out of four — answer is (b) Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap in Statement 1 targets the Attorney-General. The AG is a prominent constitutional figure (Article 76) who advises the government on legal matters, but the AG is a 'law officer' rather than a 'constitutional functionary' in the sense of the Third Schedule's coverage. Students who correctly associate the President, Ministers, MPs, Judges, and CAG with Third Schedule oaths may extend this logic to the AG, forgetting that the AG takes no such statutory or constitutional oath — they are simply appointed by the President.
solution.final_explanation:
The Second and Third Schedules define the constitutional framework for emoluments and oaths respectively. Knowing which functionaries are covered by each is a precision-testing area.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Attorney-General of India does not take an oath prescribed in the Third Schedule. The AG is a law officer (Article 76), not a constitutional office-holder in the oath sense. Third Schedule oaths cover President, VP, Ministers, MPs, MLAs, MLCs, SC/HC Judges, and CAG.
• Statement 2 — Correct: High Court Judges' salaries appear in Part D of the Second Schedule, alongside Supreme Court Judges. These are constitutionally fixed and charged to the Consolidated Fund.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Third Schedule does not provide a separately distinct oath form for MLCs versus MLAs. Article 188 requires both to take the oath, but the form in the Third Schedule covers legislature members without a separate MLC-specific variant.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Article 148(2) requires the CAG to take an oath before assuming office. The form is in the Third Schedule, confirming the CAG's constitutional standing.

Value Addition:
• The Solicitor General and Additional Solicitors General, like the AG, take no Third Schedule oath.
• Part E of the Second Schedule (CAG emoluments) and the Third Schedule (CAG oath) together comprehensively protect the CAG's independence.
• The Vice-President's oath is also in the Third Schedule, administered under Article 69.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 3 — Parliament's power to form new states, conditions and procedure
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is deceptive because students who know the President must refer state reorganization bills to affected state legislatures may assume this referral requires state legislature consent, confusing consultation with veto power.
elimination_logic: Identify the applicable provision: Article 3 empowers Parliament to form a new state from the territory of an existing state. The procedure requires the President to refer the bill to the affected state legislature for expressing its views within a specified time.

Eliminate (a): The affected state legislature does not have veto power — Parliament can proceed with reorganization even if the state legislature opposes it. State opinion is sought but is not binding.
Eliminate (c): A referendum of residents is not a constitutional requirement for state reorganization under Article 3 — this is not an Indian constitutional procedure for territorial changes.

Eliminate (d): The state legislature's recommendation is not required; only its 'views' (opinion) are sought within the time specified by the President. There is a critical difference between 'views' and 'consent.'

Confirm (b): Parliament can pass the reorganization bill by simple majority after the state legislature has been given the opportunity to express its views (within the President-specified time), even without the state's concurrence.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges 'seeking the state legislature's views' with 'requiring state legislature's consent.' Students who recall that the President must refer the bill to the affected state legislature may assume this creates a quasi-consent mechanism — that the state can block reorganization. Article 3's proviso only requires that the bill be referred to the state legislature 'for expressing views within such period as the President may specify' — Parliament can proceed with or without the views being expressed, and certainly without state consent. Options (a) and (d) both exploit this conflation.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 3 of the Constitution empowers Parliament to reorganize states. The provision is designed to preserve parliamentary supremacy over territorial questions while giving states a voice (not a veto).

Applicable principle — Article 3 proviso: No bill for state reorganization shall be introduced in Parliament except on the recommendation of the President. Before recommending, the President shall refer the bill to the legislature of the affected state for expressing its views within a specified time. Parliament is not bound by those views.

Mapping to scenario:
• A new state is to be carved out of State X's territory — Article 3 applies.
• The President must refer the bill to State X's legislature for its views.
• Once the reference period expires (with or without a state response), Parliament may pass the bill by simple majority.
• State X cannot veto the bill.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The state legislature's approval is not required; only its views are sought. Parliament can override state objections.
• Option (b) — Correct: Parliament may proceed by simple majority after the constitutional consultation procedure. No special majority or state ratification is needed.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Indian constitutional law does not require a referendum of residents for state reorganization — this is a non-existent procedural requirement.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The state legislature's 'recommendation' is not required — only its 'views' are sought, and even these are not binding on Parliament.

Value Addition:
• Laws under Articles 2 and 3 amend the First (and Fourth) Schedule by virtue of Article 4 — without invoking Article 368.
• The States Reorganisation Act 1956 is the most comprehensive exercise of Article 3 power.
• Even a state that becomes smaller due to reorganization cannot legally resist — as Andhra Pradesh experienced with the Telangana bifurcation in 2014.

Parliament proposes to bifurcate an existing state and carve out a new state from a portion of its territory. A constitutional debate arises over the procedure to be followed, particularly regarding the role of the affected state legislature and the majority required in Parliament.

Which of the following correctly describes the constitutional procedure under Article 3?

(a) Parliament can pass the reorganization bill only if the legislature of the affected state approves it by a simple majority — state legislature consent is constitutionally mandatory.
(b) Parliament may pass the reorganization bill by simple majority after the President has referred it to the affected state legislature for expressing its views within a specified time, irrespective of whether the state legislature concurs.
(c) The reorganization requires both Parliamentary legislation by special majority and a referendum among residents of the affected territory before the new state can be formed.
(d) Parliament must obtain a formal recommendation from the affected state legislature before introducing the bill; without such recommendation, the bill cannot be introduced.

solution.concept_anchor: First Amendment 1951 — Ninth Schedule creation
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) '1951, to protect industrial licensing laws' is deceptive because it gets the year correct (1951) while inserting the wrong purpose — catching students who know the year but misremember the subject matter as economic regulation rather than land reform.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The Ninth Schedule was not introduced in 1950 — the Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, and the First Amendment was passed in 1951; any option citing 1950 is incorrect.
Eliminate (b): While 1951 is correct, the purpose was to protect land reform and zamindari abolition legislation, not industrial licensing laws.
Eliminate (c): The Ninth Schedule was not introduced by the Fourth Amendment (1955), which dealt with compulsory acquisition of property and right to compensation — a related but separate amendment.

Confirm (d): The First Constitutional Amendment Act 1951 inserted Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule to shield land reform laws challenged as violating the right to property under the original fundamental rights provisions.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap in option (a) targets the year of the First Amendment. Students who know the Constitution commenced in 1950 may confuse the First Amendment (1951) with the Constitution's commencement year, selecting 1950 for the Ninth Schedule's introduction. Option (b) exploits subject-matter confusion — using the correct year but wrong subject — while option (c) attributes the Ninth Schedule to the Fourth Amendment, which was the next major property rights amendment after the First.
solution.final_explanation:
The Ninth Schedule represents one of the earliest constitutional adaptations to social reform imperatives in post-independence India.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Ninth Schedule was not part of the original Constitution of 1950. It was inserted by the First Constitutional Amendment in 1951.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: While 1951 is correct, the purpose was not industrial licensing. The amendment was driven by the need to protect zamindari abolition laws in Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, and Madras Presidency that were being struck down by courts as violations of the right to property (Articles 19(1)(f) and 31).
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Fourth Constitutional Amendment 1955 dealt with the right to compensation for compulsory acquisition and inserted further property-related protections — it did not create the Ninth Schedule.
• Option (d) — Correct: The First Constitutional Amendment Act 1951 inserted both Article 31A (saving of acquisition laws) and Article 31B (Ninth Schedule immunity) to protect land reform legislation from fundamental rights challenges.

Value Addition:
• The First Amendment also added the 'public order' and 'friendly relations with foreign states' restrictions on free speech — a wide-ranging amendment.
• The Bihar Land Reforms Act 1950 and the UP Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act 1950 were among the laws that prompted the First Amendment.
• The Ninth Schedule initially had 13 entries; it now has over 280.

(a) Introduced in 1950, to protect the original property rights provisions of the Constitution from legislative encroachment
(b) Introduced in 1951, to protect industrial licensing and economic regulatory laws from being challenged as violations of the right to trade

(d) Introduced in 1951 by the First Constitutional Amendment, to protect land reform and zamindari abolition legislation from being invalidated as violations of fundamental rights
